entries.reason: The RFC 9165 controls are not known to the cddl crate, which rejects the schema.
Hexadecimal and binary integer literals (RFC 8610 §3.5) do not parse in the cddl crate.
The b64'...' byte string literal does not parse in the cddl crate.
The cddl crate does not parse a second control after the first (`uint .ge 0 .le 150`).
The `#6.<type>(t)` form (a tag number given as a type) does not parse in the cddl crate.
`#6.N` without content and `#7.<type>` do not parse in the cddl crate.
The cddl crate overflows its stack (SIGSEGV) on a recursive rule; this library accepts it.
The unwrap operator `~` is not applied by the cddl crate, so it rejects data the unwrapped rule accepts.
`#M.N` item references (additional information N) are not applied by the cddl crate (`#7.23` is undefined, `#3.2` a two byte text string, `#0.24` a one byte argument).
`#6(t)` (any tag number) is not understood by the cddl crate.
`.cborseq` is not decoded by the cddl crate; it rejects a byte string holding the sequence 1, 2 that matches `[* uint]`.
The cddl crate accepts a value that is not a byte string for `bstr .cborseq`.
After `a = int` and `a /= tstr` the type is `int / tstr` (RFC 8610 §2.2.2); the cddl crate drops `int`.
`g //= (b: tstr)` adds a group alternative (RFC 8610 §2.2.2); the cddl crate rejects the original alternative.
The cddl crate accepts an array for `int / tstr / nil`.
`(int // tstr, tstr)` is the choice `int` or `tstr, tstr`; the cddl crate takes the comma as binding tighter than the choice differently and accepts two-element arrays that match neither alternative.
A map is closed (RFC 8610 §3.5.1): the cddl crate accepts a key the map does not list.
Same as syntax.occurrence: the cddl crate accepts a key the map does not list.
The cddl crate does not match a byte string literal key (`h'01'`) against a byte string key.

The cddl crate matches `[* int, tstr]` greedily (no backtracking), rejecting ints followed by a text string, and ignores the required `tstr`; it also treats `[[int]]` as `[int]` and accepts the flattened forms.
The cddl crate does not unescape `\n` in a text literal.
The cddl crate does not match a byte string literal against a byte string.
The cddl crate applies a numeric range to values that are not numbers (byte string) and rejects a float inside a float range.
A control narrows its target: `uint .size 1`, `tstr .size 2` and `uint .feature "f"` still require the target's type, but the cddl crate accepts values of other types.
`bstr .cbor uint` requires a byte string; the cddl crate accepts an array.
`uint .ne 5` requires an unsigned integer; the cddl crate accepts a map.
`nint` is a negative integer and `int` has no tag; the cddl crate accepts 0 for `nint` and a bignum for `int`.
`unsigned` is `uint / biguint`; the cddl crate accepts -1.
`decfrac` and `bigfloat` are tags 4 and 5 around a two-item array; the cddl crate checks neither the tag content nor the tag.
`eb64url` is tag 21 and `cbor-any` is tag 55799; the cddl crate accepts other tags.
`uri` (tag 32), `b64url` (33), `encoded-cbor` (24) and the other tagged prelude types require their tag and content; the cddl crate accepts untagged or mistyped data.
`undefined` is `#7.23` (RFC 8610 Appendix D); the cddl crate rejects the simple value.
`float16`, `float32` and `float16-32` are `#7.25` and `#7.26`, which name the encoding width (RFC 8610 §3.3); the cddl crate accepts a float64 encoding.
`number` is `int / float` (RFC 8610 Appendix D); the cddl crate rejects a float64.
`time` and `tdate` are tags 1 and 0; the cddl crate accepts untagged data.
`.and` and `.within` are enforced only around generic structures; this library accepts values the argument excludes.
`.bits` is parsed but not enforced or computed (see docs/CONFORMANCE.md).
`.det` is parsed but not enforced or computed (see docs/CONFORMANCE.md).
`.eq` is parsed but not enforced or computed (see docs/CONFORMANCE.md).
`.plus` is parsed but not enforced or computed (see docs/CONFORMANCE.md).
`.ne` is parsed but not compared.
`.cat` is not computed: `"a" .cat "b"` rejects the correct value "ab".
`tstr .cat "b"` concatenates a type with a literal; RFC 9165 defines `.cat` for literals, so what it means is not settled.
`.cborseq` is accepted without decoding the sequence; the byte string holds a text string, not unsigned integers.
The date text of `tdate` is not checked against RFC 3339.
